examples.label: nslookup - Windows TXT record via specific DNS server

notes: `dig any` is often refused by modern resolvers; query record types individually (a/mx/ns/txt/soa). TXT/SPF records leak third-party services and internal IP ranges. Always try an AXFR zone transfer against each NS. `host` is simpler than `dig` for quick A/MX/TXT lookups; `nslookup` is the Windows equivalent. Bash loops over wordlists or IP ranges provide manual brute force without needing dnsrecon/dnsenum. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 6 (Information Gathering).

recommended.note: Brute subdomains once you know the zone.
Attempt a full AXFR zone transfer.

name: DNS - dig Queries & Zone Transfer
description: Query DNS records with dig; a successful AXFR zone transfer dumps every record - internal hostnames and IPs in one shot.

defense.why_it_works: Adversaries query DNS to gather network intelligence including subdomains, mail servers, name server records, and MX/TXT/SPF records that reveal third-party services. Misconfigured DNS servers that allow zone transfers (AXFR) expose every DNS record for a domain in a single query — providing a complete map of the target's network.
defense.prerequisites: A target domain name and a resolver that will answer queries for it.
defense.impact: DNS records (A/MX/NS/TXT/CNAME) mapping the target's infrastructure and mail/hosting providers.
defense.detection: Zone transfer attempts (DNS AXFR requests) from unauthorized IPs can be logged and alerted on. General DNS reconnaissance has a high false positive rate; detection efforts are more effective when focused on related Initial Access stages that follow the reconnaissance.
defense.artifacts: DNS queries in resolver logs; high-volume querying stands out in the authoritative server's logs.
defense.prevention: Implement DNS zone transfer policies that enforce a validated list of servers permitted for AXFR transfers. Restrict zone transfers to authorized secondary DNS servers only. Remove DNS records for internal-only infrastructure from public-facing DNS.
defense.evasion: Spread queries over time and rotate source IPs to stay under server-side rate limits; use third-party passive-DNS databases (SecurityTrails, DNSDumpster) instead of direct queries to avoid generating traffic the target's DNS servers log.
defense.misconfiguration: DNS zone transfers (AXFR queries) are permitted to any requesting host — not restricted to authorized secondary DNS servers. This exposes the entire DNS zone (all hostnames, IPs, mail servers, internal naming conventions) to any attacker who can reach the DNS port. Even without AXFR, DNS servers that respond to ANY queries or provide detailed error messages leak zone structure.
